rawItems.title: 5 long lost railway stations in Cambridgeshire you may not have heard of
rawItems.content: Cambridgeshire's railway network was once far larger than it is today, with long-lost stations serving market towns, villages and growing industrial centres across the county. While many have since disappeared, their stories remain woven into the landscape, offering fascinating reminders of a very different age of travel. Before Peterborough became synonymous with the East Coast Main Line, the city's first railway station was Peterborough East. Opened in 1845 by the Eastern Counties Railway, it served routes towards Northampton, Rugby, March, Wisbech and Norwich. The station was known simply as Peterborough until being renamed Peterborough East in 1923. Passenger services ended in June 1966 as part of wider railway cutbacks, although the site continued handling parcels traffic until 1970. Today, little remains apart from the historic engine sheds, but the former station played a crucial role in shaping Peterborough's growth into a major railway city. Ramsey was once unusual in having two separate railway stations. Ramsey North opened in 1863 as the terminus of the Ramsey Railway branch from Holme. rawItems.content: Residents are being asked to help decide where a new zebra crossing should be installed in Ramsey as part of plans to improve pedestrian safety and accessibility in the town. Cambridgeshire County Council is asking residents to choose between two possible sites for the crossing. The proposed locations are: Residents have two sites to choose from one is on High Street, opposite Ramsey Abbey Gatehouse, the other is on Hollow Lane opposite Ramsey Golf and Bowls Club. (Image: Google Maps / Street View) The council said the results of the survey, which runs until midnight on Wednesday, October 28, will be considered alongside other highway, safety and accessibility information before a final decision is made. Residents, students, parents, carers and regular pedestrians are all being encouraged to take part. The council says residents’ views will help identify the safest and most effective site for people travelling on foot. An engagement survey has been opened to gather views on the proposals. Councillors have voted to refuse a controversial 199-home development plan for Ramsey despite receiving a recommendation for approval. BDW Trading Ltd submitted the proposal for land south of The Malting with landowners Susan and Robert Pickard. The scheme included up to 199 homes, 40 per cent affordable housing, children’s play areas, drainage infrastructure and related works. Developers also proposed a landscaped perimeter, a 1.1km circular walking route linked to public rights of way and green infrastructure covering around 37 per cent of the site. The site is land south of The Malting in Ramsey However, at a meeting on October 19, Huntingdonshire District Council's Development Management Committee voted to refuse the outline application, which had been recommended for approval. items.title: Cambridgeshire trio climb North Africa’s highest peak and raise £9,000 for charity
items.content: Three friends from Cambridgeshire have scaled the highest peak in North Africa. James Baker, 35, from Ramsey, Paul Mallinson, 65, from Houghton, and Tamar Mullard, 45, from Whittlesey took on Mount Toubkal in Morocco. Their five-day ascent raised more than £9,000 for Sue Ryder’s palliative, end-of-life care, and bereavement support services. Paul, Tamar and James (Image: Sue Ryder ) James said: "There is no doubt that the challenge was hard – in fact by far the hardest thing I have ever done – and exhausting." He said the trek was in memory of his father, Peter, who died from oesophageal cancer at the age of 54. James said: "Even though Dad was only in a hospice for two days, those two days were completely different from his time hospital. The hike (Image: Sue Ryder) "The hospice staff were amazing." Paul said the climb, which totalled 70,000 steps and 34 miles, was tougher than he had anticipated. Paul said: "At 70,000 steps and 34 miles, the climb and descent was longer than I expected, and I had to keep reminding myself why I was doing it."
